newsitem.title: HONG KONG: U.S. measures seen hitting HK clothing exports.
newsitem.headline: U.S. measures seen hitting HK clothing exports.

text.p: New U.S. documentation requirements imposed on Hong Kong clothing exports pose a serious threat to the territory's clothing industry, the Bank of East Asia Ltd said in a research report on Tuesday.

In June, U.S. customs announced Hong Kong manufacturers of five categories of clothing had to submit additional documents certifying Hong Kong origin when exporting to the United States, supposedly to prevent illegal transshipments from China.
An additional four categories were placed on a U.S. watchlist in September.

The U.S. measures meant manufacturers had to take more time to obtain the required documents and increased business risks for both exporters and importers, notably the chance of incurring shipment delays and penalties, the bank said.
Following protests by the Hong Kong government, the two sides agreed to conduct joint factory visits during September in a bid to resolve the dispute.
But the bank said it was not clear if the United States will drop the new measures at the end of the month.
The bank estimated the territory's total domestic exports this year would be reduced by 4.7 percent had the additional measures been called off at the end of September,
However, if the measures stayed for a prolonged period, U.S. buyers would turn to other regional manufacturers and some business with the country could be lost permanently, it said.
The worst case scenario would be for Hong Kong to lose all domestic exports to the United States, which was estimated to be 15.3 percent of total annual domestic exports, the bank said.
However, the industry could expect better times in the long term as a producer of upscale garments and as a regional marketing and design centre, it added.
After Hong Kong's return to China in 1997, economic ties with China would become closer, generating more opportunities for manufacturers to obtain bigger shares of the Chinese market.
Japan, with continuing market deregulation, would be the second best potential market for clothing manufacturers here as Hong Kong fashion was increasingly popular in Japan, it said.
